common_name: Ocean Spirit Daylily (Lavender Cascade Unusual-Form, Child of Loch Ness Monster)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this dormant diploid, registered by J.P. Murphy in 2006, carries heavy branching and a high bud count into a mid-to-late season bloom.

directions: Registered by J.P. Murphy in 2006 from a cross of (Grey Witch x Magic of Oz) and Loch Ness Monster, Ocean Spirit is a fragrant dormant diploid bearing seven-inch lavender flowers with a purple eye and a cream edge above a chartreuse throat, its petals twisting into the cascading form typical of unusual-form daylilies. Carried on 40-inch scapes with 26 buds across four branches, it blooms in the mid-to-late season and went on to collect an AHS Honorable Mention in 2011 and an Award of Merit in 2016. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain its heavy bud count.

common_name: Commandment Daylily (Orange-Pink Blend, Parent of Sombrero Way)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this dormant tetraploid, registered by Reckamp in 1968, reblooms through midseason once established.

directions: Registered by Reckamp in 1968 from a cross of Minted Gold and (Summer Splendor x Paris Gown), Commandment is a dormant tetraploid bearing bright pinkish-orange blend flowers with a green throat, about six and a half inches across on 30-inch scapes. It blooms and reblooms in midseason and earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 1972 followed by an Award of Merit in 1977, and it was later crossed with Crystal Ball to produce the 1975 President's Cup winner Sombrero Way. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Crystal Ball Daylily (Apricot-Pink Blend, Parent of Sombrero Way)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this fragrant dormant tetraploid, registered by Reckamp in 1969, reblooms through its early-midseason display.

directions: Registered by Reckamp in 1969, Crystal Ball is a fragrant, reblooming dormant tetraploid bearing apricot-pink blend flowers with a deeper-toned throat, about six inches across on 26-inch scapes that open in the early midseason. It was later crossed with Commandment to produce Sombrero Way, winner of the 1975 President's Cup. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor.

common_name: Copper Lantern Daylily (Yellow Ochre Eyezone, Parent of Orange Velvet)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this dormant diploid, registered by Joiner in 1982, blooms in midseason once clumps are established.

directions: Registered by Joiner in 1982 from a cross of Emerald Crown and Colonel Simon, Copper Lantern is a dormant diploid bearing yellow-ochre flowers about six inches across marked with a chrome-yellow eyezone above a green throat, carried on 30-inch scapes that bloom in midseason. It was later crossed with Golden Scroll to produce the 1999 Lenington All-American Award winner Orange Velvet. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain bloom production.

common_name: Arms Reaching Out Daylily (Soft Yellow with Rose-Red Eye, Parent of Mayor of Cornatzer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this fragrant evergreen diploid, registered by N. Eller in 2004, reblooms through its early-midseason display.

directions: Registered by N. Eller in 2004 from a cross of Big Kiss and Sanford Show Girl, Arms Reaching Out is a fragrant, reblooming evergreen diploid bearing soft yellow flowers with a rose-red eye above a yellow throat, opening nearly 95 percent double on 24-inch scapes carrying 18 buds across three branches. It earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 2009 and was later crossed with Beware the Wizard to produce the Ida Munson Award winner Mayor of Cornatzer. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain its double form.

common_name: Beware the Wizard Daylily (Orange-Red Spider-Double, Parent of Mayor of Cornatzer)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this semi-evergreen diploid, registered by G. Couturier in 1995, blooms in midseason on tall scapes.

directions: Registered by G. Couturier in 1995 from a cross of Double Bow Tie and Firestorm, Beware the Wizard is a semi-evergreen diploid spider-form daylily with an eight-inch bloom at a 4.4-to-1 petal ratio, colored orange-red and marked with a dark red eyezone above a gold throat, its heavily polymerous flowers often producing extra petal segments. Carried on 37-inch scapes that open in midseason, it was later crossed with Arms Reaching Out to produce the Ida Munson Award winner Mayor of Cornatzer. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Cherry Valentine Daylily (Bright Pink with Crimson Eye, Parent of Mary Alice)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this evergreen tetraploid, registered by Trimmer in 1999, reblooms through its early-season display.

directions: Registered by Trimmer in 1999 from a cross of (Ruby Sentinel x tetraploid Enchanting Blessing) and tetraploid Dragon's Eye, Cherry Valentine is an evergreen tetraploid bearing bright pink flowers about four inches across with a crimson-red eyezone above a green throat, carried on 28-inch scapes with 30 buds across three branches that open and rebloom in the early season. It earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 2004 and was later crossed with Siloam Ralph Henry to produce the 2009 President's Cup winner Mary Alice. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Midnight Glamour Daylily (Chrome Yellow Self, Parent of Lolabelle)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this semi-evergreen diploid, registered by G. Lenington in 1962, blooms in the early midseason.

directions: Registered by G. Lenington in 1962, Midnight Glamour is a semi-evergreen diploid bearing a chrome-yellow self flower on 36-inch scapes that open in the early midseason. It was later used in a cross that produced the 1968 President's Cup winner Lolabelle, whose nocturnal, unusual-form bloom habit traces back to this older yellow self. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering.

common_name: Majestic Gold Daylily (Gold Self, Parent of Golden Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this reblooming evergreen diploid, registered by Guidry in 1988, blooms in the early season.

directions: Registered by Guidry in 1988, Majestic Gold is a reblooming evergreen diploid bearing a gold self flower with a green throat, about four and a half inches across on 23-inch scapes that open in the early season. It earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 1991 and was later used in a cross that produced the 2003 President's Cup winner Golden Hibiscus. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain heavy bloom.

common_name: So Lovely Daylily (Near-White Self, Parent of After Awhile Crocodile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this semi-evergreen diploid, registered by G. Lenington in 1969, blooms in midseason.

directions: Registered by G. Lenington in 1969, So Lovely is a semi-evergreen diploid bearing a near-white self flower with a green throat, about five and a half inches across on 30-inch scapes that open in midseason. It earned an AHS Honorable Mention in 1974 and was later crossed with Olallie Lois to produce the 2005 Eugene S. Foster Award winner After Awhile Crocodile. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Olallie Lois Daylily (Dark Wine with Lighter Eyezone, Parent of After Awhile Crocodile)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; this dormant diploid, registered by Darrow in 1981, blooms in the mid-to-late season.

directions: Registered by Darrow in 1981, Olallie Lois is a dormant diploid bearing a dark wine flower with a lighter eyezone above a yellow-green throat, about four and a half inches across on 28-inch scapes that open in the mid-to-late season. It was later crossed with So Lovely to produce the 2005 Eugene S. Foster Award winner After Awhile Crocodile. Plant divisions in full sun in well-drained soil, dividing congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.
